comments: β numerical validation — Monte Carlo check of the analytical variance
formula for the octonion associator, Fano-triple case.
Setup (per docs/research/variance_of_associator.md § "Worked example:
single Fano generator"):
A(a, b, c) := ‖[a, b, c]‖²   where [a,b,c] = (a·b)·c − a·(b·c)
Unperturbed: [a,b,c] = 2·e_7, A = 4.
Perturb a_1 → 1 + δ, δ ~ N(0, σ²). The analytical first-order GUM
variance (from the β document, derivation):
Var(A) ≈ 64 σ²                                (TRUTH)
If the current compiler's stepwise scalar-product rule were applied
instead, it would give:
Var_compiler(A) ≈ 16 σ²                       (COMPILER, 4× low)
This test computes the sample variance of A over N = 100,000 Monte
Carlo samples and compares to the TRUTH formula. It does NOT test the
compiler's variance_of() — that requires the full Knowledge<f64>
chain which introduces unrelated complexities (see ζ buffer bug). The
compiler comparison is deferred to a separate test.
Pass criterion: |MC_var − 64σ²| / 64σ² < 0.05 (5% relative error).
If this passes, β's analytical formula is validated empirically. The
remaining claim — that the compiler produces 16σ² — is then a
separate reading-confirmation task.

comments: ep_sqrt must be a square root across the whole f64 range, not only near 1.
It used to run ten Heron steps from y = x. Heron converges quadratically only
once the iterate is near the root; from y = x it first needs ~log2(sqrt(x))
halving steps just to get close, so a fixed step count silently bounds the
range over which the result is a square root at all.
Measured 2026-09-09 before the fix, as relative residual |y*y - x| / x:
Accurate only for x in about [1e-4, 1e4] and catastrophically wrong outside,
which reached ep_std, ep_sqrt_ep, ep_rel_uncertainty and ep_budget -- all of
them thin wrappers over ep_sqrt(variance). A variance of 1e-6, an ordinary
measurement uncertainty, made ep_std report a standard deviation 29.6% off.
The oracle here is the residual, not a table of expected digits: y is a
square root of x exactly when y*y == x to within rounding, and that is
checkable without an external sqrt (ADR-008 keeps the oracle in Sounio).
Tolerance is 1e-12 relative. After the fix the measured residual is at most
~1 ulp (2.2e-16) at every point below -- exactly 0 only where x is a perfect
square in f64 -- so the bound leaves ~4 orders of magnitude of slack while
still being ~7e11 times tighter than the old behaviour at 1e6.
It is deliberately NOT an equality check. y*y == x holds for 1, 4, 1e6 and
the other f64-representable squares, and fails for 2 (residual 2.2e-16), 3
and 1e-6. A first draft of this file's notes claimed a residual of 0
everywhere; that was truncation in the measurement, not exactness, and the
mandatory math-review offload caught it.

//@ run-pass
//@ expect-stdout-contains: PASS
//
// Native-stage mirror for the F1 Moufang/alternativity smoke. The original
// import-bearing program is parked under tests/madaros/ocssm_imported/.

fn embed_axis(hash: i64) -> i64 {
    let r: i64 = hash - (hash / 7) * 7
    return 1 + r
}

fn embed_into(hash: i64, out: &![f64; 8]) with Mut {
    var i: i64 = 0
    while i < 8 {
        out[i as usize] = 0.0
        i = i + 1
    }
    out[0] = 0.6
    out[embed_axis(hash) as usize] = 0.8
}

fn oct_mul(a: &[f64; 8], b: &[f64; 8], out: &![f64; 8]) with Mut, Div, NonAssoc {
    var r0 = a[0] * b[0]
    r0 = r0 - a[1] * b[1]
    r0 = r0 - a[2] * b[2]
    r0 = r0 - a[3] * b[3]
    r0 = r0 - a[4] * b[4]
    r0 = r0 - a[5] * b[5]
    r0 = r0 - a[6] * b[6]
    r0 = r0 - a[7] * b[7]
    out[0] = r0

    var r1 = a[0] * b[1] + a[1] * b[0]
    r1 = r1 + a[2] * b[3] - a[3] * b[2]
    r1 = r1 + a[4] * b[5] - a[5] * b[4]
    r1 = r1 - a[6] * b[7] + a[7] * b[6]
    out[1] = r1

    var r2 = a[0] * b[2] + a[2] * b[0]
    r2 = r2 - a[1] * b[3] + a[3] * b[1]
    r2 = r2 + a[4] * b[6] - a[6] * b[4]
    r2 = r2 + a[5] * b[7] - a[7] * b[5]
    out[2] = r2

    var r3 = a[0] * b[3] + a[3] * b[0]
    r3 = r3 + a[1] * b[2] - a[2] * b[1]
    r3 = r3 + a[4] * b[7] - a[7] * b[4]
    r3 = r3 - a[5] * b[6] + a[6] * b[5]
    out[3] = r3

    var r4 = a[0] * b[4] + a[4] * b[0]
    r4 = r4 - a[1] * b[5] + a[5] * b[1]
    r4 = r4 - a[2] * b[6] + a[6] * b[2]
    r4 = r4 - a[3] * b[7] + a[7] * b[3]
    out[4] = r4

    var r5 = a[0] * b[5] + a[5] * b[0]
    r5 = r5 + a[1] * b[4] - a[4] * b[1]
    r5 = r5 - a[2] * b[7] + a[7] * b[2]
    r5 = r5 + a[3] * b[6] - a[6] * b[3]
    out[5] = r5

    var r6 = a[0] * b[6] + a[6] * b[0]
    r6 = r6 + a[1] * b[7] - a[7] * b[1]
    r6 = r6 + a[2] * b[4] - a[4] * b[2]
    r6 = r6 - a[3] * b[5] + a[5] * b[3]
    out[6] = r6

    var r7 = a[0] * b[7] + a[7] * b[0]
    r7 = r7 - a[1] * b[6] + a[6] * b[1]
    r7 = r7 + a[2] * b[5] - a[5] * b[2]
    r7 = r7 + a[3] * b[4] - a[4] * b[3]
    out[7] = r7
}

fn oct_associator(a: &[f64; 8], b: &[f64; 8], c: &[f64; 8], out: &![f64; 8]) with Mut, Div, NonAssoc {
    var ab: [f64; 8] = [0.0; 8]
    var ab_c: [f64; 8] = [0.0; 8]
    var bc: [f64; 8] = [0.0; 8]
    var a_bc: [f64; 8] = [0.0; 8]
    oct_mul(a, b, &!ab)
    oct_mul(&ab, c, &!ab_c)
    oct_mul(b, c, &!bc)
    oct_mul(a, &bc, &!a_bc)
    var i: i64 = 0
    while i < 8 {
        out[i as usize] = ab_c[i as usize] - a_bc[i as usize]
        i = i + 1
    }
}

fn norm_sq(v: &[f64; 8]) -> f64 {
    return v[0]*v[0] + v[1]*v[1] + v[2]*v[2] + v[3]*v[3]
         + v[4]*v[4] + v[5]*v[5] + v[6]*v[6] + v[7]*v[7]
}

fn alt_stat_sq(x: &[f64; 8], y: &[f64; 8]) -> f64 with Mut, Div, Panic, NonAssoc {
    var assoc: [f64; 8] = [0.0; 8]
    oct_associator(x, x, y, &!assoc)
    let den_sq: f64 = norm_sq(x) * norm_sq(x) * norm_sq(y)
    if den_sq < 0.0000000000000001 { return 0.0 }
    return norm_sq(&assoc) / den_sq
}

fn main() -> i64 with IO, Mut, Div, Panic, NonAssoc {
    var hashes: [i64; 8] = [100, 200, 100, 300, 200, 400, 300, 500]
    var sum: f64 = 0.0
    var count: i64 = 0
    var i: i64 = 0
    while i < 8 {
        var j: i64 = i + 1
        while j < 8 {
            if hashes[i as usize] == hashes[j as usize] {
                var x: [f64; 8] = [0.0; 8]
                var y: [f64; 8] = [0.0; 8]
                embed_into(hashes[i as usize], &!x)
                embed_into(701 + i + j, &!y)
                sum = sum + alt_stat_sq(&x, &y)
                count = count + 1
            }
            j = j + 1
        }
        i = i + 1
    }

    var ok: i64 = 1
    var stat_sq: f64 = 0.0
    if count > 0 { stat_sq = sum / (count as f64) }
    if count == 0 { ok = 0 }
    if stat_sq >= 0.000000000000000000000001 { ok = 0 }

    if ok == 1 { print("PASS\n") } else { print("FAIL\n") }
    return 0
}

comments: Regression test (segfault landmine, discovered via PR #2058):
A string literal passed as a function-call argument is embedded directly
in the generated code with a "jmp over the bytes, then lea rax back at
them" trick. The x86-64 codegen used a rel8 (single signed byte, -128..127)
displacement for that skip jump. Any literal whose decoded content was
>= 127 bytes made the skip distance overflow the byte, wrapping negative
and sending execution backward into unrelated, already-emitted code --
corrupting whatever ran next. The callee was never reached; the crash hit
while the *caller* was still setting up the argument.
This exercises a literal well past that threshold (~200 bytes) as a call
argument, and checks the callee receives the exact content -- not just
that the process survives.

instruction: Write a Sounio run-pass example named `tuple_return_sret_r12_slot`. A tuple-returning function that CALLS another tuple-returning function used to destroy its caller's aggregate-return pointer. The x86 SRET prologue is `push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; push r12; sub rsp,frame`, so. It should compile and run successfully. Expected stdout: TUPLE_SRET_R12_OK
description: A tuple-returning function that CALLS another tuple-returning function used to destroy its caller's aggregate-return pointer. The x86 SRET prologue is `push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; push r12; sub rsp,frame`, so
comments: A tuple-returning function that CALLS another tuple-returning function used to
destroy its caller's aggregate-return pointer.
The x86 SRET prologue is `push rbp; mov rbp,rsp; push r12; sub rsp,frame`, so
the saved r12 lives at rbp-0x08 -- which was also slot 1, where the incoming
SRET pointer was stored. `pop r12` then restored that pointer instead of the
caller's r12, and the caller wrote its result through a pointer into the
callee's dead frame. The next call reused those bytes, so every binding read
the LAST call's values.
Confirmed under gdb: r12 intact at the callee's entry, holding the callee's
own SRET at its `ret`. Fixed by reserving slot 1 for the pushed r12.
Two bindings minimum: with one, a stale pointer still reads its own values.

comments: Finding 11 (issue #2084): const_prop folds u64 >>, /, % with unsigned
semantics — without this, fold_binop_int would treat operands as i64

Witnesses 4 cases that all hit the literal-only fold path (no binary
IR ever gets emitted for these expressions; they compile to IrLoadImm
via const_prop ->  cp_u64_div / cp_u64_mod / cp_u64_shr):
0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF_u64 /  2   == 0x7FFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF   (cp_u64_div)
0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF_u64 >> 4   == 0x0FFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF  (cp_u64_shr)
0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF_u64 >> 64  == 0                      (cp_u64_shr, n>=64)
The equality comparisons then anchor the folded values at runtime.
Under the signed fold path these would each be a different number:
0xFFFF.. / 2  = 0          in i64 truncate-toward-zero
0xFFFF.. % 3  = -1         in i64 truncate-toward-zero
0xFFFF.. >> 4 = 0xFFFFFFFF in i64 arithmetic shift
0xFFFF.. >> 64 = (out of range, BOTTOM -> no fold)
and each assert below would catch that signed result.
